# Check if the column in df2 is of string type and only convert if it contains the % symbol
if df2['Proportion of schools with no sanitation service'].dtype == 'object':
    # Try to check if the first non-null value is a string and contains %
    sample_value = df2['Proportion of schools with no sanitation service'].dropna().iloc[0] if not df2['Proportion of schools with no sanitation service'].dropna().empty else None

# Figure 1: World map - Distribution of child poverty rates
# Use GeoPandas and plotnine to draw a map
# Load world map data - Use the downloaded Natural Earth data
world = gpd.read_file('ne_110m/ne_110m_admin_0_countries.shp')

# Merge the dataset with the map data - Use ISO codes
map_data = world.merge(df1, left_on='ISO_A3', right_on='alpha_3_code', how='left')

# Create a simple map (Note: plotnine is not very suitable for complex map drawing, but it can be simply displayed)
p1 = (ggplot() +
      geom_map(map_data, aes(fill='Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards')) +
      scale_fill_cmap('OrRd', name='Child triple poverty rate') +
      labs(title='Global distribution map of child triple poverty rate') +
      theme_minimal() +
      theme(figure_size=(15, 10)))
display(p1)
# Save Chart 1
p1.save(os.path.join(output_dir, '1_world_map.png'), width=15, height=10, dpi=300)

This world map illustrates the global distribution of child triple poverty rates. Overall, significant disparities exist across different regions. In Africa, some countries have extremely high poverty rates; for instance, those in the red - colored areas have a child triple poverty rate of 0.3, the highest globally, highlighting that children in parts of Africa face severe multi - dimensional poverty. In Asia, certain regions also exhibit relatively high poverty rates. For example, in some South Asian countries, the rate ranges from 0.1 to 0.2, indicating that populous areas in Asia still face challenges in alleviating child poverty. Regions like Europe, North America, and Australia mostly appear gray, signifying that the child triple poverty rates in these areas are relatively low. This shows that the global child poverty situation is highly uneven. Parts of Africa and Asia need to intensify poverty - reduction efforts, and the international community should provide more attention and assistance to improve the current situation of child poverty.¶

# Find the top 10 countries with the highest poverty rates
top10_countries = df1.sort_values('Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards', ascending=False).head(10)
top10_countries['country'] = pd.Categorical(top10_countries['country'], 
                                            categories=top10_countries['country'][::-1], 
                                            ordered=True)

# Use plotnine to draw a bar chart - Simplified way, without using reorder
p2 = (ggplot(top10_countries, aes(x=pd.Categorical(top10_countries['country'], categories=top10_countries['country'], ordered=True), 
                          y='Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards')) +
 geom_bar(stat='identity', fill='#FF5733', width=0.7) +
 coord_flip() +
 labs(title='Top 10 countries with the highest child triple poverty rates',
      x='Country',
      y='Child triple poverty rate') +
 theme_minimal() +
 theme(figure_size=(12, 8), 
       plot_title=element_text(size=14),
       axis_text_y=element_text(size=11)))
display(p2)
# Save Chart 2
p2.save(os.path.join(output_dir, '2_top10_countries.png'), width=12, height=8, dpi=300)

Top 10 Countries with the Highest Child Triple Poverty Rates¶

This chart showcases the ten countries with the highest child triple poverty rates globally. Ethiopia leads the list, with its child triple poverty rate approaching or possibly exceeding 0.3. Chad, Niger, and other countries closely follow, all with poverty rates well above 0.2. Nations like Madagascar, Papua New Guinea, and Mozambique have poverty rates ranging from 0.2 to 0.3. Cambodia and Benin have relatively lower but still significant rates, around 0.2. Most of these countries are concentrated in Africa and parts of Asia, indicating that these regions face substantial challenges in combating child poverty. Urgent international attention and resource allocation are required to improve the situation of children living in poverty.

# Figure 3: Scatter plot - Relationship between life expectancy and poverty rate (with prediction line), using numpy to implement linear regression
# Merge the datasets to obtain the required variables
poverty_life = df1[['country', 'alpha_3_code', 'Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards', 'obs_life expectancy']]
poverty_life = poverty_life.dropna()

# Use numpy to implement simple linear regression
x = poverty_life['Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards'].values
y = poverty_life['obs_life expectancy'].values
x = x.reshape(-1, 1)  # Convert to a two-dimensional array for matrix calculation

# Add an intercept term
X = np.hstack([np.ones((x.shape[0], 1)), x])

# Use the normal equation to calculate the coefficients
beta = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y

# Calculate the predicted values
poverty_life['predicted'] = beta[0] + beta[1] * poverty_life['Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards']

# Use plotnine to draw a scatter plot and a regression line
p3 = (ggplot(poverty_life) +
 aes(x='Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards', 
     y='obs_life expectancy') +
 geom_point(aes(color='obs_life expectancy'), size=3, alpha=0.7) +
 geom_line(aes(y='predicted'), color='red', size=1) +
 scale_color_gradient(low='blue', high='red') +
 labs(title='Relationship between child poverty rate and life expectancy',
      x='Child triple poverty rate',
      y='Life expectancy (years)',
      color='Life expectancy') +
 theme_minimal() +
 theme(figure_size=(10, 8)))
display(p3)
# Save Chart 3
p3.save(os.path.join(output_dir, '3_poverty_life_correlation.png'), width=10, height=8, dpi=300)

The relationship between the child triple poverty rate and life expectancy. A clear negative correlation is evident. As the child triple poverty rate increases from nearly 0 to around 0.3, life expectancy drops from approximately 80 years to about 50 years. The red line in the graph further emphasizes this trend. Red dots represent areas with higher life expectancy, while blue dots indicate areas with lower life expectancy. This implies that in regions with a high child poverty rate, the life expectancy of residents tends to be low. This may be due to adverse factors such as scarce medical resources and insufficient nutrition resulting from poverty, which affect health and thus lower life expectancy. This conclusion highlights the significance of reducing the child poverty rate for improving the population's life expectancy, providing crucial reference for policymakers in poverty alleviation and enhancing people's livelihoods.¶

# Figure 5: Box plot - Comparison of child poverty rates in different continents
# Merge the dataset with the metadata to obtain continent information
map_data_continent = map_data[['country', 'CONTINENT', 'Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards']].dropna()

# Use plotnine to draw a box plot
p5 = (ggplot(map_data_continent, aes(x='CONTINENT', y='Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards', fill='CONTINENT')) +
 geom_boxplot(width=0.7, show_legend=False) +
 scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda l: [f'{v:.0%}' for v in l]) +
 labs(title='Comparison of the distribution of child triple poverty rates in different continents',
      x='Continent',
      y='Child triple poverty rate') +
 theme_minimal() +
 theme(figure_size=(12, 8),
       axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1)))
display(p5)
# Save Chart 5
p5.save(os.path.join(output_dir, '5_continent_comparison.png'), width=12, height=8, dpi=300)

This box - and - whisker plot illustrates the distribution of child triple poverty rates across different continents. Africa has the highest child triple poverty rate, with most of the box ranging from 10% to 20%, and there are some outliers above 20%, indicating that many areas in Africa face severe child triple poverty issues. Asia follows, with the poverty rate box generally between 0% and 10%. North and South America have relatively lower child triple poverty rates. North America's box is concentrated at lower levels, and South America's box has a smaller range with even lower values. Europe and Oceania have the lowest child triple poverty rates, with a more concentrated distribution and generally small values. Overall, there are significant differences in child triple poverty rates among continents, and Africa faces the most prominent challenges, requiring focused attention and targeted poverty - reduction measures.¶

# Figure 6: Heat map - Correlation between child poverty rate and other socioeconomic indicators
# Merge the data to analyze the correlation
merged_data = df1.merge(df_meta, on=['country', 'alpha_3_code', 'year'], how='inner')

# Select relevant indicators
indicators = ['Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards', 
             'GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)', 
             'Life expectancy at birth, total (years)',
             'Birth rate, crude (per 1,000 people)',
             'Hospital beds (per 1,000 people)']

corr_data = merged_data[indicators].corr()

# Convert the correlation matrix to a long format for plotnine
corr_long = corr_data.reset_index()
corr_long = pd.melt(corr_long, id_vars='index')
corr_long.columns = ['Indicator1', 'Indicator2', 'Correlation']

# Create a dictionary mapping for shorter labels
indicator_labels = {
    'Percentage Children suffering exactly three deprivation. Homogeneous moderate standards': 'Child poverty rate',
    'GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)': 'GDP per capita', 
    'Life expectancy at birth, total (years)': 'Life expectancy at birth',
    'Birth rate, crude (per 1,000 people)': 'Crude birth rate',
    'Hospital beds (per 1,000 people)': 'Hospital beds per 1,000 people'
}

corr_long['Indicator1'] = corr_long['Indicator1'].map(indicator_labels)
corr_long['Indicator2'] = corr_long['Indicator2'].map(indicator_labels)

# Use plotnine to draw a heat map
p6 = (ggplot(corr_long, aes(x='Indicator1', y='Indicator2', fill='Correlation')) +
 geom_tile() +
 scale_fill_gradient2(low='blue', mid='white', high='red', midpoint=0) +
 geom_text(aes(label='round(Correlation, 2)'), size=10) +
 labs(title='Heat map of the correlation between child poverty rate and socioeconomic indicators',
      x='',
      y='',
      fill='Correlation coefficient') +
 theme_minimal() +
 theme(figure_size=(10, 8),
       axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1)))
display(p6)
# Save Chart 6
p6.save(os.path.join(output_dir, '6_indicators_correlation.png'), width=10, height=8, dpi=300)

This heat map shows the correlations between the child poverty rate and several socio - economic indicators. There is a strong negative correlation ( - 0.87) between the child poverty rate and life expectancy at birth, indicating that the longer the life expectancy, the lower the child poverty rate, likely because a better - health environment helps reduce poverty. It also has a negative correlation ( - 0.66) with hospital beds per 1,000 people, suggesting that more abundant medical resources are associated with a lower child poverty rate. The negative correlation ( - 0.67) with GDP per capita implies that a higher level of economic development corresponds to a lower child poverty rate. Conversely, the child poverty rate has a strong positive correlation (0.89) with the crude birth rate, meaning that a higher crude birth rate is associated with a higher child poverty rate, perhaps due to the increased support burden from a high birth rate exacerbating poverty. These correlations reveal the significant influence of socio - economic factors on child poverty, providing multi - dimensional references for formulating poverty - reduction policies.¶
